index.title: Learn tarot: free beginner guides · ShenTarot
index.description: Free tarot lessons for beginners: how to read tarot cards, the Major and Minor Arcana, the four suits, numbers, court cards, reversals and how to ask a good question.
index.lead: Seven short guides take you from your first shuffle to reading a full spread on your own. Read them in order, or jump to the one you need.

page.title: {title} · ShenTarot
page.practiceText: Draw a card on the site and read it with what you just learned.

how-to-read-tarot.title: How to read tarot cards: a beginner's guide
how-to-read-tarot.description: How to read tarot cards step by step: ask a clear question, shuffle, lay out a spread, read each card in its position and link the cards into one story.
how-to-read-tarot.answer: To read tarot, ask one clear question, shuffle, lay the cards in a spread, read each card in its position, then look at how the cards connect.

sections.h: What a tarot reading is
p: A tarot deck has 78 cards. Each card is a picture of a common human situation: a new start, a loss, a choice, a celebration. In a reading you draw a few cards and use them as prompts to look at your question from new angles.
Most people today read tarot for reflection rather than prediction. The cards don't decide anything for you. They help you notice what you already feel and think about what you could do next.

sections.h: Step 1: ask one clear question
p: Good readings start with good questions. Open questions about you work best, such as "What do I need to understand about my job?" rather than "Will I get fired?". Our guide to [asking tarot questions](learn/asking-questions) shows how to turn a worry into a question the cards can answer.

sections.h: Step 2: shuffle and draw
p: Shuffle in any way that feels natural while you think about your question. When you feel ready, stop and draw cards from the top, or cut the deck and draw from where it splits. There is no single correct method, so pick one and keep using it.

sections.h: Step 3: lay out a spread
p: A spread is a pattern in which each position has a meaning. Beginners do well with a [single card](spreads/single) for a daily focus, or the [three-card spread](spreads/three) for past, present and future. Once these feel easy, try the [Celtic Cross](spreads/celtic).

sections.h: Step 4: read each card in its position
p: Look at the picture first. Who is in it, what are they doing, and how does it feel? Then read the card's meaning on its [card page](cards) and ask how it fits the position. The Five of Cups in a "past" position points to a loss you have been through, while in an "advice" position it asks you to turn toward what remains.
If a card lands upside down, you can read it reversed. Our [guide to reversals](learn/reversed-cards) explains the simple ways to do that.

sections.h: Step 5: link the cards into one story
p: Now step back. Are there many cards of one suit? Lots of [Cups](learn/tarot-suits) put feelings at the centre, and lots of Major Arcana mean a big life theme. Do the numbers rise or repeat? Do the figures face toward or away from each other? These links turn single meanings into one story.
Finish by summing up the reading in one or two sentences, and write it down. Coming back to old readings is one of the fastest ways to learn.

sections.h: How to practise
p: Draw one card each morning and guess how it might show up in your day. Check in the evening. The [card of the day](tools/daily-card) tool does this for you, and after a few weeks you will know most of the deck without looking anything up.

faq.q: Can anyone read tarot?
faq.a: Yes. Reading tarot is a skill you learn by practising with the pictures and meanings. You don't need any special gift.

faq.q: Do I need to memorise all 78 cards?
faq.a: No. Start by learning the 22 Major Arcana and the meaning of the four suits and the numbers. With those, you can work out most Minor Arcana cards on your own.

faq.q: How many cards should a beginner draw?
faq.a: One to three. A single card or a three-card spread is easy to read in depth, and you learn more from three cards read well than ten read quickly.

major-and-minor-arcana.title: Major and Minor Arcana: structure, differences and a worked example
major-and-minor-arcana.description: Compare 22 Major and 56 Minor Arcana, check the historical sources, and connect the Magician with the Eight of Pentacles without treating card ratios as a prediction.
major-and-minor-arcana.answer: The deck used here has 22 Major Arcana and 56 Minor Arcana. Those counts describe its structure; “big themes” and “everyday situations” are teaching lenses, not measures of importance or fate.

sections.h: Two groups: what can be counted
p: In this illustrated 78-card system, 22 cards belong to the Major Arcana. The remaining 56 form four suits, each with ten cards from Ace to Ten and four court cards: Page, Knight, Queen and King. Waite describes these divisions in Part I, §§2–3. This lesson concerns that system, not every historical or modern deck.

sections.h: Major Arcana: 22 images, not 22 guaranteed life events
p: In the deck shown on this site, [the Fool](cards/major-00-fool) bears 0 and [the World](cards/major-21-world) bears 21. Their numbering helps identify cards. Following a sequence can be a memory exercise, but it does not establish that your life must follow those stages. Waite’s Part II also discusses different placements of the Fool; do not confuse numbering with a single historical reading order.

We sometimes use a Major card to ask about a broader value or assumption. That is an interpretive choice. A Major card can also be useful for an ordinary decision; it need not signal a lasting event or something beyond your control.

sections.h: Minor Arcana: four suits, fourteen cards each
p: The four [suits](learn/tarot-suits) are Wands, Cups, Swords and Pentacles. Ten pip cards plus four [court cards](learn/court-cards) make fourteen per suit: 4 × 14 = 56. Read the particular picture and spread position rather than assigning every Minor card the same role.

For teaching, we may connect these images with actions, feelings, thoughts and resources. That does not make them less important, faster-changing or more controllable than Major cards. A small practical detail can be central to the question.

sections.h: What a ratio can—and cannot—tell you
p: Counting Major cards describes the spread you drew. In this guide we do not use “more than half” as evidence of a turning point, outside forces or a fixed timescale. First ask what each position means and how the images connect. A large count is not an instruction to surrender your judgment.

sections.h: Original example: connect a theme with an action
p: Observation: [the Magician](cards/major-01-magician) has a raised wand and the four suit emblems on the table (Waite, Part II, §2, I). [The Eight of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-eight) shows a craftsperson at work (Part III, §2, Pentacles—Eight). These descriptions are the source-based starting points, not proof that a project will succeed.

Reasoning: for “How can I restart a creative project?”, put the Magician in “What can I use?” and the Eight in “What can I try?”. The first image invites a resource inventory; the second suggests using one resource in a repeatable practice. Try one tool for ten minutes, then note what helped. That action is our original teaching inference, not Waite’s instruction.

Alternative: if the Magician occupies “What distracts me?”, attention to tools could suggest collecting equipment instead of practising. If the Eight occupies a challenge position, repetition could suggest over-polishing rather than useful progress. Check the question and actual circumstances. One Major plus one Minor does not establish which concern matters more.

sections.h: Sources and their scope
p: [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part I](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_1), §§2–3: the Major/Minor division, four suits, ten pip cards and four court cards per suit. The 56-card total is the arithmetic of that structure.

[Part II](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_2), §1 and §2 (I, 0, XXI): variation in the Fool’s placement, the Magician’s table and the Fool/World labels. [Part III](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3), §2, Pentacles—Eight: the working craftsperson. These passages document descriptions and a historical tradition, not empirical predictions or our project example.

The consulted Wikisource transcription is the 1922 reprint, whose title pages list first publication in 1910. We use it for the passages above, not as an endorsement of every occult or divinatory claim in the book.

faq.q: How many Major Arcana cards are there?
faq.a: There are 22 in the illustrated system used here. This deck labels the Fool 0 and the World 21; other decks and printed ordering conventions can differ.

faq.q: Are Major Arcana cards more important?
faq.a: Not automatically. Importance comes from the question, position and the connections you find. A Minor card may carry the most useful detail, and a Major card does not prove an external event will occur.

faq.q: Can I read with only the Major Arcana?
faq.a: You can choose the 22 Major cards for a focused practice. State that choice before drawing, and remember that the result no longer samples the full 78-card deck. It is an exercise, not proof that only Major cards are sufficient for every question.

tarot-suits.title: The four tarot suits: sources, questions and a worked example
tarot-suits.description: Learn Wands, Cups, Swords and Pentacles as reading prompts, check the elemental convention, and follow an original Four of Wands/Four of Cups example.
tarot-suits.answer: Wands, Cups, Swords and Pentacles organize the 56 Minor Arcana. Their themes and elements are interpretive conventions: useful prompts, not a formula for events, personality or health.

sections.h: Four groups, not half a meaning
p: This deck has four suits of fourteen cards: Ace to Ten and four court cards, for a total of 56. Waite describes the structure in Part I, §3. A suit helps compare cards, but it does not supply “half” a meaning. Check the [number](learn/tarot-numbers), [court rank](learn/court-cards), picture and spread position together.

Here we use Wands–Fire, Cups–Water, Swords–Air and Pentacles–Earth. The four Ace titles in Liber LXXVIII explicitly use those pairings. This documents one correspondence system, not a natural law or a rule for every deck. Its designs are not interchangeable with this site’s card images.

sections.h: Four suits as questions you can try
p: Wands: what would I like to begin or practise? Energy and initiative are our teaching prompts. With the [Ace of Wands](cards/wands-ace), name one small action you can actually try, then notice what makes starting easier.

Cups: what am I noticing about connection or feeling? With the [Two of Cups](cards/cups-two), compare what you give and receive in one interaction. Separate what you observed from what you are assuming.
Swords: which thought, decision or boundary needs attention? With the [Ace of Swords](cards/swords-ace), write one clear question and distinguish what you know from what you still need to ask.

Pentacles: what resources, work or practical support are involved? The family and house in the [Ten of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-ten) can prompt an inventory of shared time, space and tools. Which arrangements are already agreed, and which need a conversation?

sections.h: Check the picture before using a keyword
p: Compare the [Four of Wands](cards/wands-four) and [Four of Cups](cards/cups-four). Waite describes a garland on four staves with two figures holding flowers, and a seated person beneath a tree with three cups and another offered (Part III, §2, the two Four entries). The number is shared; the scenes differ. Neither “Four means stability” nor a suit label explains the whole picture.

sections.h: What a suit balance does not establish
p: Counting suits describes the cards drawn. Missing Cups do not prove that you suppress feelings, and many Swords do not diagnose a condition or predict an argument. Ask whether an observation is useful for your actual question rather than using counts to label yourself or someone else.

Our [elemental dignities](tools/elements) tool applies a correspondence model to compare cards. “Support” and “opposition” are labels inside that model, not measured physical forces or probabilities of success. You can set that model aside when it obscures the image or question.

sections.h: Original example: planning a small gathering
p: Observation: the Four of Wands presents a garlanded setting and flower-bearing figures; the Four of Cups presents a seated figure and an offered cup. Those details can be checked in Waite. The following gathering scenario is our teaching example, not a reported client reading or a historical instruction.

Reasoning: ask “How can I plan time with friends that suits me?”. Put the Four of Wands in “What can I prepare?” and the Four of Cups in “What should I check with myself?”. One possible link is a simple welcoming setting plus an honest check of your capacity before accepting plans. A small action: propose one manageable activity and say what time you can give.

Alternative: in “What pressures me?”, the garland could invite reflection on an expectation to celebrate; in “What can help?”, the seated figure could suggest pausing before saying yes. Compare these possibilities with your circumstances. The cards cannot tell you how your friends feel or guarantee that a meeting will go well.

sections.h: Sources and their limits
p: [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part I](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_1), §3: four suits, ten pip cards and four court cards each. This supports the deck structure, not a fixed percentage of a card’s meaning.

[Liber LXXVIII, The Titles of the Symbols](https://sacred-texts.com/oto/lib78.htm), items 1–4: the Ace titles pair Wands with Fire, Cups with Water, Swords with Air and Pentacles with Earth. This is a primary text of a correspondence tradition; it does not verify the system as a physical mechanism or make its pictures identical to Waite–Smith designs.

[Waite, Part III](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3), §2: Four of Wands, Four of Cups, Two of Cups, Ace of Swords and Ten/King of Pentacles. We checked the scene descriptions and the limits of money-only readings. The consulted Waite transcription is the 1922 reprint. Our teaching questions and gathering example are original applications, not validated predictions.

faq.q: Which suit is about love?
faq.a: Cups can prompt questions about feelings and reciprocity in this teaching approach. Any suit can contribute to a relationship question; none proves another person’s feelings or a future relationship.

faq.q: Which suit is about money?
faq.a: Pentacles can help you reflect on resources and work. A suit or card is not evidence of future income, secure wealth or a suitable financial decision.

faq.q: Are Swords bad cards?
faq.a: Not as a fixed label. Look at the particular scene, your question and its position. Swords are not a diagnosis, a prediction of conflict or a reason to call someone a bad person.

tarot-numbers.title: Numbers in tarot: a learning aid, not a fixed rule
tarot-numbers.description: Learn Ace-to-Ten keywords, see why cards with the same number differ, and follow a sourced Five of Cups example with an alternative interpretation.
tarot-numbers.answer: Numbers can help you compare cards, but do not determine their meaning. Use them as memory prompts, then check the picture, suit and spread position.

sections.h: Use numbers as prompts, not a formula
p: Our Ace-to-Ten list is a ShenTarot learning aid, not a universal law or a table quoted from Waite. A number may suggest a theme; the [suit](learn/tarot-suits), image and position can change it. Five plus Cups can prompt a question about disappointment, but the [Five of Cups](cards/cups-five) also shows what remains.

sections.h: Ace to Ten: ShenTarot memory prompts
p: Ace: a new beginning, a gift or a raw chance.
Two: a choice, a partnership or a balance to keep.
Three: first growth, teamwork or results.
Four: stability, rest or holding on.
Five: conflict, loss or a test.
Six: recovery, harmony and give-and-take.
Seven: reflection, challenge or standing your ground.
Eight: movement, effort and change.
Nine: near completion, either fulfilment or worry before the end.
Ten: the end of a cycle, its full reward or its full weight.

sections.h: Reading numbers in a spread
p: Repeated numbers invite comparison rather than a forecast. Three Aces need not mean three events, and high numbers do not prove that a situation is almost over. Ask what the images share and where they differ.

In this deck, the Major Arcana are numbered 0 to 21. Our [birth-card](tools/birth-card) and [year-card](tools/year-card) tools use separate digit-sum conventions explained on their pages; calculation is not evidence that dates predict events.

sections.h: Why the same number is not the same meaning
p: Waite describes moving wands in the Eight of Wands, a bound and blindfolded woman in the Eight of Swords, and a craftsperson working in the Eight of Pentacles (Part III, §2, the three card entries). “Eight means action” cannot account for all three pictures. Compare [Eight of Wands](cards/wands-eight), [Eight of Swords](cards/swords-eight) and [Eight of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-eight) before choosing an interpretation.

sections.h: Original example: what is still available after a setback?
p: Observation: in the Five of Cups, three cups lie fallen and two remain standing behind the cloaked figure. Waite describes both loss and something remaining (Part III, §2, Cups—Five). These are the source observations; the reflection below is our teaching example, not a prediction or a historical quotation.

Reasoning: for the position “What can help me resume a project?”, attention to the fallen cups may suggest disappointment, while the standing pair invites an inventory of resources still available. One possible action is to name a skill, person or tool you can still use. The number five helps recall tension; it does not supply that action on its own.

Alternative: in a challenge position, the same picture might ask whether counting what remains is making you hurry past a real loss. Pause rather than force a positive reading. Check which interpretation fits the question; neither tells you what another person thinks or what will happen.

sections.h: Sources and what they support
p: [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part III](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3): §1 explains why numbers and bare keywords are insufficient; §2 contains the Five of Cups and the three Eight descriptions used above. This supports descriptions and one historical interpretive tradition, not scientific prediction or every keyword in our learning table.

[Edition information](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot): the consulted transcription identifies a 1922 reprint and lists first publication in 1910, with designs by Pamela Colman Smith. We do not present it as the 1910 first-edition scan.

faq.q: What does an Ace mean in tarot?
faq.a: In this learning aid, an Ace prompts a question about an opportunity in its suit. Check the image and position; a new event is not guaranteed.

faq.q: Are Fives always difficult?
faq.a: Challenge is a useful prompt in our learning table, not a rule for every deck or reading. Compare the actual image: loss with something remaining in the Five of Cups differs from the contest in the Five of Wands. Context can change what you take from either card.

faq.q: Do court cards have numbers?
faq.a: In this deck, Page, Knight, Queen and King have rank titles rather than the Ace-to-Ten sequence. Read image and suit; this article assigns no universal number.

court-cards.title: Tarot court cards: ranks, sources and a worked example
court-cards.description: Learn the sixteen court cards through sourced images and practical questions. Compare two Knights and follow a Page/Knight of Pentacles example with another possible reading.
court-cards.answer: This deck has sixteen court cards: Page, Knight, Queen and King in each suit. Ranks can organize reflection, but do not identify a real person’s gender, age, character or intentions.

sections.h: Four ranks in four suits
p: Four [suits](learn/tarot-suits) each contain four courts, giving 4 × 4 = 16 in this deck. Waite describes King, Queen, Knight and Knave/Page in Part I, §3. Titles and arrangements can differ between systems. Read the image as well as the rank rather than treating a title as a personality result.

sections.h: Four questions to try
p: Page: what could I learn or notice? With the [Page of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-page), choose something small to examine closely and write one question about it. This is a teaching prompt, not a rule that every Page is a child or a student.

Knight: what pace suits the task? Compare the [Knight of Wands](cards/wands-knight) and [Knight of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-knight) before choosing a next step. A rank alone does not tell you to rush.

Queen: what deserves attentive care or listening? With the [Queen of Cups](cards/cups-queen), describe what you can actually notice in a conversation before offering a response. Anyone can try this question; it is not a definition of women or an “inner” nature.

King: what decision or responsibility is mine? With the [King of Swords](cards/swords-king), state a boundary or criterion and explain it clearly. This is a practice question, not evidence that a particular man is authoritative or trustworthy.

sections.h: Two Knights, different pictures
p: Waite describes the Knight of Wands as on a journey and makes the horse’s motion part of the description. The Knight of Pentacles rides a slow, enduring, heavy horse (Part III, §2, the two Knight entries). That contrast challenges “all Knights rush”. Use the scene to refine the [suit](learn/tarot-suits) prompt rather than assigning one speed to every Knight.

Waite also describes the Queen of Cups as seeing and acting (Part III, §2, Cups—Queen). The source itself gives more than a passive “inner” role. Our rank prompts are choices for practice, not a complete description of every Queen or King.

sections.h: A person, a role or an approach?
p: If a figure reminds you of someone, name the behaviour you observed and the question it raises. Recognition is an association, not proof that the card identifies them or reveals their motives. You can also use the same picture to consider a role you are taking or an approach you might try.

The [which card are you](tools/which-card-are-you) quiz is a playful matching exercise based on your answers. Its result is not a validated personality assessment. Treat it as a prompt to consider, not a label to keep.

sections.h: Original example: learning at a sustainable pace
p: Observation: Waite’s Page of Pentacles looks intently at a pentacle above raised hands; his Knight of Pentacles holds the symbol while riding the slow, heavy horse (Part III, §2, Pentacles—Page and Knight). Those are source descriptions. The following skill-learning scenario is our original exercise, not a client case or a quotation.

Ask “How can I make room to learn this skill?”. Place the Page in “What needs my attention?” and the Knight in “How can I continue?”. One possible link is close observation followed by a repeatable pace: pick one basic technique, try a short session and choose a realistic time to return. Write what you noticed rather than judging whether you match a rank.

Alternative: with the Page in “What keeps me preparing?”, close study might suggest postponing a first attempt; with the Knight in “What needs adjusting?”, slowness might ask whether the routine has become rigid. Compare the two stories with your circumstances. Neither card establishes your ability, personality or eventual result.

sections.h: Sources and scope
p: [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part I](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_1), §3: four court ranks per suit, including the Knave/Page terminology and the relation of rank to suit. This supports the structure, not claims about which cards beginners find hardest or what most readers believe.

[Part III](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3), §2: Knight of Wands, Knight/Page of Pentacles, Queen of Cups and King of Swords. We checked the named scene descriptions. The four practice questions and learning scenario are editorial applications, not historical instructions or independently validated personality categories.

The consulted transcription is Waite’s 1922 reprint. Its historical descriptions of people are not evidence for identifying living people by sex, age, appearance or moral character. This guide does not apply those categories as a test of you or anyone else.

faq.q: Do court cards always mean a person?
faq.a: Not necessarily. In this guide, person, role and approach are possibilities to explore. Thinking of a familiar person does not prove that the card describes them or knows their intentions.

faq.q: Does a King mean a man and a Queen mean a woman?
faq.a: No gender assignment is required in this practice. Anyone can consider care, judgment, learning or pacing. Historical titles and figures do not determine the gender or character of a person you know.

faq.q: How many court cards are in a tarot deck?
faq.a: This illustrated deck has sixteen: Page, Knight, Queen and King in each of four suits. Other systems may use different titles or arrangements.

reversed-cards.title: Reversed tarot cards: sources, questions and a worked example
reversed-cards.description: Read reversals without automatic opposites or promised outcomes. Compare three Waite entries, try optional questions and follow an original two-card example.
reversed-cards.answer: A reversal records that a card is upside down. How you interpret it depends on the convention you choose, the picture and the question; it does not automatically mean the opposite, a bad outcome or a guaranteed delay.

sections.h: Start with the orientation, then choose a convention
p: A reversed card is upside down relative to your chosen reading direction. Before drawing, decide whether to distinguish orientations or read every card upright. For this exercise, either is an available choice. Write it down so you do not change the rule just to get a more welcome answer.

sections.h: Four questions you can try
p: Blocked: what makes this quality difficult to put into practice? With the [Ace of Wands](cards/wands-ace), you might ask what would let a small creative idea get started. This is our practice prompt, not a universal definition of a reversal.
Inward: what do I notice in my own response? With [the Hermit](cards/major-09-hermit), compare chosen time alone with feeling cut off. Do not assume the card diagnoses either.

Too much or too little: what needs adjusting? With [Strength](cards/major-08-strength), consider whether your approach needs more patience or a firmer boundary, then compare that thought with observable circumstances.

Timing: is there a practical obstacle I can check? A reversal cannot establish that an event is promised or will arrive later. Choose a useful question rather than treating all four lenses as facts about the draw.

sections.h: Three historical entries that resist one rule
p: In Waite’s Part III, §3, [the Sun](cards/major-19-sun) reversed retains the upright sense to a lesser degree. [The Tower](cards/major-16-tower) reversed includes a reduced version of its difficult meaning, but also oppression and confinement. That does not establish that a crisis has been avoided.

Part III, §2 gives reversed [Ten of Swords](cards/swords-ten) a possible advantage or success that does not last. It does not guarantee recovery. These different entries support comparing each card, not a rule that reversals always improve, worsen or negate it. Historical fortune-telling lists are not evidence that an event will happen.

sections.h: Keep the orientation visible while practising
p: In the [reading workspace](read), choose a card and set its reversed checkbox to match your physical draw. Read the question and position alongside the orientation; you can compare the card page’s upright and reversed sections. Recording a choice does not validate its meaning. If you are practising upright-only, leave the checkbox clear rather than changing it after seeing the result.

sections.h: Original example: making practice enjoyable again
p: Observe [the Sun](cards/major-19-sun), whose child and white horse Waite describes in Part II, §2, and the working craftsperson in [Eight of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-eight), Part III, §2. In this invented exercise the Sun is reversed in “What deserves attention?” and the Eight is upright in “What can I try?”. The pictured objects remain the same when the card is turned.

Ask “What could make my hobby practice more enjoyable this week?”. Borrowing the Sun’s reduced positive sense as a prompt, one possible reading is that satisfaction feels muted; the Eight suggests trying a manageable piece of hands-on practice. Choose one small technique you want to try and note what you actually enjoy. That is an editorial inference and an action to test, not Waite’s instruction or a client story.

Alternative: if you are already practising too much, the Eight may draw attention to repetitive work rather than invite more of it. Try a shorter session or a break and compare the result. Neither orientation tells you your emotional state, promises improvement or decides how much effort is right for you.

sections.h: Sources and their limits
p: [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part III](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3), §2 (Ten of Swords; Eight of Pentacles) and §3 (Sun; Tower), supports the specific historical comparisons above. The four questions are our teaching options; this check does not establish how commonly readers use them.

[Part II](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_2), §2, XIX, supports the Sun image description. The consulted transcription is the 1922 reprint. Source descriptions, historical meanings and our hobby example serve different purposes; none supplies a verified prediction.

faq.q: Do I have to read reversed cards?
faq.a: No. For this exercise you can choose upright-only or distinguish orientations. Decide beforehand and record the choice; no popularity claim or special predictive advantage is established here.

faq.q: Is a reversed card always negative?
faq.a: No single good/bad rule fits the historical entries compared here. Start with the card, position and question rather than assigning a result from its orientation alone.

faq.q: How do I get reversed cards when shuffling?
faq.a: For a physical-deck exercise, you can rotate part of the deck before mixing it. Keep the same viewing direction when laying out the cards. This introduces different orientations; it does not prove that a draw carries a message.

asking-questions.title: How to ask tarot questions: scope, sources and a worked example
asking-questions.description: Frame a question for reflection, distinguish historical methods from our suggestions, and follow an original three-card example without promises about the future.
asking-questions.h1: How to ask tarot a question
asking-questions.answer: For a reflection exercise, ask about a situation you can describe and a next step you can examine. Open questions are our teaching choice, not proof that cards know the answer or read someone else’s mind.

sections.h: A question gives the exercise a focus
p: Write what you want to explore before drawing. “What can I try in this situation?” gives you a task for comparing the picture with your experience. It does not make the draw evidence about hidden facts. Feeling worried or wording a question imperfectly does not make you responsible for a confusing reading.

sections.h: Three choices that keep the task manageable
p: Name your part: “What could I say in a conversation with my partner?” leaves room for a real response instead of assuming you know their feelings. Keep the scope small: separate moving home from changing jobs if you want to examine them separately. Prefer “what” or “how” for this exercise because you can write several possibilities; we have not established that they produce more accurate or richer readings.

sections.h: Questions you can adapt
p: Relationship: “What do I want to explain, and what should I ask rather than assume?”. Work: “What example of my work can I prepare for our next conversation?”. Choice: “What information is missing, and what could I check?”. Our [decision spread](spreads/three-decision) uses situation, challenge and a way forward, not one guaranteed future per option. More prompts are in the [question guides](questions). For health, legal or financial decisions, consult an appropriate professional. Tarot is for reflection and entertainment, not professional advice.

sections.h: What the historical source actually says
p: Waite’s Part III, §7 introduces a method for a definite question, includes yes-or-no legal examples and allows a repeat in specified circumstances. That records his method; it does not validate its predictions or supply legal guidance. Our open-question preference and suggestion to pause before repeating are editorial choices, not universal rules attributed to him. A [yes-or-no tool](tools/yes-no) result is not external evidence of an answer.

sections.h: Original example: starting a small hobby project
p: Change “Will my project succeed?” to “With two hours this weekend, what small part could I try?”. Use situation, challenge and way forward with three upright cards: [the Magician](cards/major-01-magician), [Two of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-two) and [Eight of Pentacles](cards/pentacles-eight). Waite describes four suit symbols on the Magician’s table, a dancing figure holding two pentacles, and a craftsperson at work. Those are source descriptions; this project is an invented exercise.

One possible connection: the Magician prompts an inventory of materials already available; the Two, in the challenge position, prompts a look at competing demands; the Eight suggests one practical technique. Choose a small sample you can make within the two hours, set aside one competing task if possible, and note what you learned. This is our reasoning from positions and pictures, not a prediction or a client success story.

Alternative: if materials and time are already sufficient, the same sequence might draw attention to collecting tools instead of beginning. Try using one existing tool before buying or planning more. Write what fits and what does not in the [reading workspace](read), then compare it with what actually happens. If you revisit the question, keep the first notes and say what changed rather than treating a new draw as a correction of reality.

sections.h: Sources and limits
p: [A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Part II](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_2), §2, I, supports the Magician’s table and four suit symbols. The inventory prompt is our application, not a quoted instruction.

[Part III](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Pictorial_Key_to_the_Tarot/Part_3), §2 (Two and Eight of Pentacles) supports the other picture descriptions; §7 supports the historical question and repeat-method comparison. We consulted the 1922 reprint transcription. These passages do not establish reader outcomes, access to private thoughts or a proven best wording.

faq.q: Can I ask tarot yes or no questions?
faq.a: You can use a yes-or-no format, but its output is not proof about the world. This lesson uses open questions to generate possibilities you can examine; it does not establish superior prediction.

faq.q: Can I ask about another person?
faq.a: You can reflect on an interaction, but a card does not establish another person’s thoughts or consent. Name what you observed and what you could ask them directly.

faq.q: Can I ask the same question twice?
faq.a: There is no universal prohibition established here. For this exercise, pause, keep the original notes and identify what changed or what new question you want to explore. Another draw is not evidence that the first or second answer is true.
